q: The two questions behind almost every packaging problem are
options: Which Python is running, and what can it import
why: `sys.executable` and `module.__file__` answer them in one line each.

options: A directory with its own `site-packages` and its own `python`
A copy of the standard library
why: Activating just puts its `bin` first on `PATH`, which is why `which python` tells you whether it worked.

q: `python -m pip install x` is preferable to `pip install x` because
options: It installs into the interpreter you named rather than whichever `pip` the shell found
why: That one habit prevents most "but I installed it" conversations.

options: Creates an executable that imports a module and calls a function, written `module:function`
Lists scripts to run at install time
why: The entire mechanism behind every command-line tool you have installed with pip.

why: Every pin is a constraint on everybody who depends on you, and two libraries pinning a third differently cannot coexist.

options: In a lock file, not in `pyproject.toml`
why: `pyproject.toml` says what you can work with; the lock file says what you did.

options: Every direct and transitive dependency at one version, and is committed and generated
What you edit when you upgrade
why: Recording only what you named leaves the resolver free to pick differently underneath.

q: `importlib.metadata.version("myapp")` is preferable to a hand-written `__version__` because
options: There is then one version number, in `pyproject.toml`, rather than two that drift
why: A project that must keep `__version__` should have a three-line test asserting the two agree.
